strengths: The paper is technically solid and well-executed: a multiscale graph-based diffusion model (MeshGraphNet-style architecture with EDM preconditioning and GenCast-style norm conditioning) is applied to generative data assimilation on genuinely unstructured, industrial-scale meshes (~3e5 nodes) of a real urban neighbourhood (Bristol, UK) at Re ~ 2e7, which is a demanding and practically relevant setting.

The formulation of classifier-free guidance as tempered posterior sampling (Eq. 5) is clearly articulated and connects the generative approach to classical DA weighting between background and observation terms; the ablation over gamma (Appendix C.1) supports this interpretation empirically.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: comparisons against two supervised GNN baselines and a non-learned reduced-order DA baseline (LCSVD), three metrics (RRMSE, SSIM, MAC), multiple sensor densities, and robustness tests under three sensor-sampling strategies (random, cloud, trajectory) that represent a distribution shift in the observation operator.
The test protocol holds out two altitude slices with different obstacle configurations and mesh topologies, so the reported generalization is not merely interpolation over wind directions.

Reproducibility is aided by a detailed appendix: full hyperparameters, training configuration (200k steps, 4x A100, batch sizes), sampling settings (T=20, gamma=2.0), graph statistics, and formal metric definitions.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the framework is essentially a combination of established components (multiscale MeshGraphNets, EDM diffusion, CFG, GenCast conditioning). The 'CFG as tempered posterior sampling' interpretation is close to known results on guided diffusion for inverse problems (e.g., Gao et al. 2025, cited but not compared against), and the paper presents it with somewhat more novelty than warranted.

Missing key baselines: Diff-SPORT (Vishwasrao et al., 2025), which is directly relevant diffusion-based reconstruction in urban environments, is discussed in the introduction but not compared against. Similarly, no diffusion-based inverse-problem baseline (e.g., DPS-style guidance) or comparison to Gao et al. 2024 is provided, making it hard to isolate what the proposed multiscale CFG formulation contributes beyond generic guided diffusion.

The claimed benefit of ensemble-based, uncertainty-aware inference is never evaluated: no calibration, spread, or coverage metrics are reported despite the abstract and conclusions repeatedly invoking uncertainty quantification as an advantage over deterministic baselines.

The notion of 'generalization across unseen geometries' is weak: all six slices come from the same neighbourhood, differing only by altitude. True cross-geometry generalization (different building layouts/cities) is asserted in the framing but not tested.

Ground truth is steady RANS mean fields only; measurement noise (eta in Eq. 1) is defined but never tested, and the 2D slice restriction plus steady-flow assumption limits the practical significance of claims about real-time environmental monitoring with mobile sensors.

Table 2 (sampling-strategy robustness) reports GenDA only, without baselines, so it is unclear whether the moderate degradation is better or worse than alternatives under clustered/trajectory observations.

No computational cost comparison: inference requires T=20 guided sampling steps on a 3e5-node graph; runtime versus the GNN baselines and LCSVD is not reported, which matters for the claimed real-time monitoring use case.

Reproducibility gaps: no code release is mentioned, and several dataset pointers are incomplete in the text ('Further details... are available at', 'More information can be found at'), leaving the data source under-specified.

Improvements in the hardest regime (300 observations) are modest relative to LCSVD (~14% RRMSE reduction), and statistical significance of the differences is not discussed given the overlapping standard deviations in Table 1.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: reconstructing high-resolution urban wind fields on large, unstructured meshes (~3x10^5 nodes) from very sparse sensors, using an industrial-scale RANS dataset of a real Bristol neighbourhood (Re ~ 2x10^7).

The empirical evaluation is reasonably thorough within its scope: three sensor densities, three sampling strategies (random, cloud, trajectory), three metrics (RRMSE, SSIM, MAC), an ablation of the CFG weight gamma, and hold-out of two altitude slices as unseen geometries. GenDA shows consistent and substantial gains (e.g., RRMSE 0.190 vs 0.353-0.354 at 3000 observations).

The multiscale graph hierarchy (o2o/o2r/r2r/r2o edge sets with geometry-aware decimation preserving building footprints) is a sensible engineering contribution for scaling diffusion to large meshes, and architectural details are documented in the appendix (EDM preconditioning, norm conditioning, hyperparameters).
The robustness experiments under clustered and trajectory-based observation patterns, despite training only with random placement, are a useful robustness check relevant to real deployments.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the framework is a direct combination of well-established components - multiscale MeshGraphNets (Fortunato et al., 2022), EDM (Karras et al., 2022), GenCast-style conditioning (Price et al., 2024), and CFG as posterior/tempered sampling, which is already known in the inverse-problem literature. The main conceptual claim (CFG as tempered posterior sampling) is an interpretation rather than a new method, and closely builds on Giral et al. (2025) by what appears to be an overlapping group.

The theoretical framing is heuristic and not rigorously supported. CFG with gamma > 1 does not sample from the true posterior; the tempered-posterior view (Eq. 5) ignores well-known failure modes of guidance (samples leaving the prior manifold, biased score estimates under strong conditioning). No analysis of when this approximation is valid is provided, and the claimed analogy to classical DA weighting is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Claims of generalization are overstated: the 'unseen geometries' are merely other horizontal slices of the same urban neighbourhood. The paper claims generalization 'across unseen geometries, wind directions, and mesh resolutions without retraining', but no experiment tests a genuinely different urban layout, and mesh-resolution generalization is never evaluated.

Uncertainty quantification is claimed as a key benefit ('uncertainty-aware ensembles') but never evaluated: there is no calibration, coverage, or spread-vs-error analysis of the ensemble samples. This is an unsupported central claim.

The data setting weakens the significance: fields are steady RANS mean fields with only 360 wind directions per slice, i.e., a low-dimensional, strongly correlated family. The paper does not discuss whether a full diffusion model is necessary for such a narrow distribution, nor how the approach would handle unsteady or turbulent fluctuation fields.

No comparison against alternative diffusion-based posterior samplers (e.g., DPS-style guidance, or the sparse-reconstruction guidance of Amorós-Trepat et al. and Oommen et al. that the paper itself cites), so it is unclear what the specific CFG-based conditioning contributes versus other assimilation-via-diffusion approaches.

Computational cost is not reported: sampling latency with T=20 steps on a ~3x10^5-node graph versus the baselines, nor training cost (200k steps on 4x A100), which matters for the claimed real-time monitoring motivation.

Observation noise is absent: sensors read noise-free ground-truth values, and the measurement model (Eq. 1) is never instantiated or tested with realistic noise; robustness to noisy or biased sensors is not studied.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or data release is mentioned; several references are incomplete mid-sentence ('More information can be found at', 'database are available at'), the loss weighting lambda(sigma) is not specified, and LCSVD baseline configuration details are thin. The near-identical LCSVD/Table 2-cloud entries (0.354/0.834/0.918) suggest possible copy-paste errors in the tables.

Baseline fairness is not fully established: the supervised GNN baselines are deterministic regressors trained on the same data, but there is no discussion of whether they were given the same observation-mask input conditioning or tuned comparably, making the magnitude of claimed gains (25-57% RRMSE reduction) harder to interpret.

strengths: The evaluation is conducted on an industrially realistic dataset: high-fidelity RANS simulations of a real Bristol neighbourhood at Re ≈ 2×10^7, with complex geometry, and generalization is tested on genuinely held-out mesh slices (z=35, 40 m) not seen during training, which is a more demanding test than random splits.

The multiscale graph formulation (o2o/o2r/r2r/r2o edge sets with boundary-preserving decimation) is well motivated and well documented; Appendix B.2/B.3 provides enough architectural and training detail (EDM preconditioning, noise schedule, sensor-dropout probability p_uc=0.1, guidance weight) to make reproduction plausible.

The tempered-posterior reading of classifier-free guidance (Eq. 5) is a clean and useful framing that connects the sampling procedure to classical DA background/observation weighting, and the gamma ablation (Appendix C.1) empirically supports the prior/likelihood-balance interpretation.

The evaluation covers practically relevant sensing scenarios beyond the training distribution (clustered 'cloud' sensors, mobile trajectories), and Table 1 shows consistent RRMSE/SSIM/MAC gains over MGN, MS-MGN, and a non-learned LCSVD baseline, with the largest gains in the sparse regime, which is the practically important setting.

Honest scoping of limitations in places: the paper acknowledges that only random sampling matches the training distribution, that the work is 2D and steady (RANS mean fields), and lists temporal dynamics and 3D extension as future work.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the individual components (EDM preconditioning [Karras 2022], multiscale MeshGraphNets [Fortunato 2022], sensor-dropout classifier-free guidance, GenCast-style conditioning) are all established, and the 'CFG as tempered posterior sampling' interpretation already exists in the guided-diffusion inverse-problem literature (and is closely related to Gao et al. 2025, Amorós-Trepat et al. 2025, Diff-SPORT), which the paper cites but does not empirically compare against.

The headline claim of 'generalization across unseen geometries' is overstated: all test slices come from the same Bristol neighbourhood at different altitudes, so the test geometries are structurally correlated with training geometries. Generalization to a genuinely new city or building layout is not demonstrated, yet this claim appears in the abstract, contributions, and conclusions.

Uncertainty quantification is claimed as a key advantage ('produces ensembles... support uncertainty-aware inference') but is never evaluated: there is no spread-skill, CRPS, or calibration analysis anywhere in the paper, so this central selling point is unsupported.

Missing relevant baselines: no diffusion-based inverse-problem/assimilation baseline (e.g., a diffusion posterior-sampling method applied to the same data), making it hard to isolate whether gains come from CFG guidance specifically versus simply having a strong generative prior.

Some quantitative evidence is weaker than the prose suggests: at 300 observations GenDA's SSIM (0.834) is essentially identical to LCSVD (0.831), yet the abstract advertises '23-33% SSIM improvement' by ranging over the weaker GNN baselines; no significance tests are reported, and LCSVD rows at 3000 and 8000 observations are identical to three decimals (RRMSE 0.354±0.124), which is unexplained and suspicious.

Figure 7 shows reconstruction metrics that vary only slightly across gamma in [0,5], yet the text claims a clear optimum at gamma in [1.5, 2.5] and characterizes gamma=1 as 'consistently suboptimal'; the plotted evidence does not obviously support this narrative strength of the posterior-sampling interpretation.

Computational cost is never quantified: no inference time or sampling cost comparison against the supervised GNN baselines or LCSVD, despite the motivation being real-time monitoring where expensive CFD is impractical; a 20-step diffusion sampler on ~3×10^5-node meshes may not be cheap.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: two references end with dangling sentences ('More information can be found at' on pages 3 and 11), no code or data release is stated, and the MGN baselines' training protocol (e.g., whether they saw variable sensor masks) is under-specified, which matters for fairness of the comparison.
The contribution is confined to 2D slices of steady RANS mean fields, so the framing toward 'real-time air quality monitoring pipelines in cities' is aspirational rather than demonstrated.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: GenDA is compared against three complementary classes of baselines (deterministic GNNs MGN/MS-MGN, reduced-order DA methods LCSVD/POD-3DVar, and a stochastic diffusion baseline MultiMesh-VP that shares the same multiscale backbone), which allows the authors to isolate the contribution of the classifier-free guidance (CFG) formulation from the graph architecture and diffusion modeling

Thoughtful ablations and diagnostics: the CFG weight sweep (Appendix C.1, Table 5), the single-mesh ablation of the multiscale hierarchy (Table 8), held-out sensor interpolation (Table 3), and uncertainty evaluation via CRPS and Wasserstein distances (Tables 6-7) collectively support the paper's interpretation of CFG as a controllable posterior-balancing mechanism

The problem setting is realistic and practically relevant: RANS simulations of a real Bristol neighborhood at Re ~ 2e7 on large unstructured meshes (~3e5 nodes), with multiple practical sensor deployment strategies (random, clustered, trajectory-based) and a held-out sensor protocol that tests interpolation at unseen measurement locations

The multiscale graph hierarchy (fine/reduced mesh with o2o/o2r/r2r/r2o edge sets) is well motivated for propagating sparse observations across complex geometry, and the ablation shows it matters most in the sparse-observation regime

Writing and presentation are generally clear; training, sampling, and architecture details are documented at a level that supports reproducibility (hyperparameters in Appendix B.3), and the limitations (2D steady slices, single neighborhood, no hard PDE constraints) are honestly acknowledged in the conclusions and impact statement
weaknesses: Limited novelty: all components are established — EDM preconditioning (Karras et al.), MeshGraphNets-style multiscale message passing (Fortunato et al.), CFG with sensor-dropout, and the 'CFG as (tempered) posterior sampling' interpretation is largely a known reframing rather than a new result. The closest prior work (Giral et al., 2025 for geometry-conditioned urban graph diffusion; Diff-SPORT for diffusion-based urban flow reconstruction) is acknowledged, and the delta over Giral et al. is primarily adding observation conditioning plus evaluation, which weakens the contribution's originality for a main-track venue

The generalization claims are overstated relative to the evidence. 'Generalization to held-out mesh geometries' amounts to two held-out altitude slices (z=35, 40 m) extracted from the same urban neighborhood as the training slices; the building layouts and flow statistics of test and training slices are closely related, so transfer to genuinely new cities or geometries remains untested despite abstract-level language suggesting broader applicability

Observation noise is never evaluated. Eq. (1) explicitly includes measurement noise η, and the DA framing centers on noisy sparse observations, yet all experiments use noiseless node-interpolated ground-truth values — a significant gap for a paper claiming a data assimilation contribution for real deployments (the impact statement itself flags sensor noise/bias as an open deployment issue)

The 'tempered posterior' interpretation (Eq. 5) is heuristic: no conditions are given under which CFG yields an actual tempered posterior (e.g., Gaussian likelihood structure), and there is no theoretical or empirical validation that the sampled ensembles approximate p(u|y,G)^(likelihood^gamma) beyond qualitative arguments; the framing is more narrative than formal

Baseline results show suspicious artifacts: LCSVD and POD-3DVar report nearly identical RRMSE at 3000 and 8000 observations (0.354/0.354 and 0.368/0.367), which is unexplained and could indicate saturation, implementation issues, or a reporting error; the paper should explain why these baselines do not improve at all with 2.7x more data

The guidance weight gamma=2.0 is chosen empirically, and Table 5 shows it is not optimal at all densities (best is 1.5 at 8000 obs, 3.0 at 300 obs), raising a mild concern that hyperparameter selection partially relied on the same test distribution being reported; a principled or validation-based selection procedure would be more convincing

No computational cost comparison: diffusion sampling with T=20 CFG steps requires two denoiser evaluations per step, versus a single deterministic forward pass for MGN/MS-MGN; inference latency and memory are important for the real-time monitoring motivation in the introduction but are not reported

Uncertainty evaluation (CRPS) is reported only for GenDA; without CRPS for MultiMesh-VP (which also produces ensembles), it is unclear whether the CFG formulation also improves probabilistic calibration rather than just point accuracy
The code is referenced only as a placeholder 'code link', limiting verifiability at review time

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the paper reports results across observation densities (300–8000), three sensor-sampling strategies, held-out altitude slices, a held-out sensor interpolation protocol, ensemble/uncertainty metrics (CRPS, Wasserstein distances), and ablations of both the CFG mechanism (Table 5, Figure 7) and the multiscale graph hierarchy (Table 8). This is well beyond the minimum needed to support the empirical claims.

The MultiMesh-VP baseline (same multiscale backbone, direct observation conditioning, no CFG) is a well-designed control that partially isolates the contribution of the proposed guidance formulation rather than the architecture or diffusion modeling alone.

The problem setting (sparse-observation reconstruction of urban wind fields on unstructured meshes at industrial scale, Re ≈ 2×10^7) is practically relevant and underexplored relative to structured-grid work.

Writing and organization are clear; the limitations section is honest, explicitly acknowledging restriction to steady 2D slices of a single neighborhood, absence of hard physics constraints, and the need for validation against real measurements. The impact statement appropriately frames deployment risks.

The interpretive framing of CFG guidance weight γ as analogous to background/observation weighting in classical DA is a useful conceptual bridge for practitioners, and the γ-sweep empirically demonstrates the prior/likelihood trade-off.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The paper combines established components: a multiscale MeshGraphNets-style backbone (Fortunato et al., 2022), EDM diffusion preconditioning (Karras et al., 2022), and classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans), applied to a dataset and prior model from the authors' closely related prior work (Giral et al., 2025). The delta over Giral et al. is essentially adding sensor conditioning via CFG, and Diff-SPORT (Vishwasrao et al., 2025) already applies diffusion-based urban flow reconstruction. The core 'CFG as tempered posterior sampling' observation is also well known in the inverse-problem literature (e.g., Gutha et al., 2025, cited by the authors themselves), and no new theory is provided.

The theoretical interpretation is loose. Equation (5) claims CFG samples from a tempered posterior p(u|G)p(y|u)^γ, but CFG with a learned conditional denoiser and γ>1 only approximates this under strong assumptions (exact conditional scores, guidance applied to the full score rather than the denoiser output, Gaussian likelihood with known noise). The paper presents this as an interpretation without derivation, error analysis, or discussion of when the approximation breaks; the instability at γ=3.0 and 8000 observations (RRMSE 0.481) is consistent with the approximation failing, but this is not analyzed.

Generalization claims are overstated. The 'held-out mesh geometries' are two altitude slices of the same Bristol neighborhood; buildings, terrain, and overall city structure are shared between train and test. The paper is careful to describe this as transfer 'within the studied urban-flow distribution' in some places, but the abstract and contributions imply broader geometry generalization ('held-out mesh geometries... without retraining') that the single-city, within-neighborhood evaluation does not support.

Reduced-order baselines (LCSVD, POD-3DVar) rely on linear subspaces that the introduction itself argues are ill-suited to geometry changes, making these comparisons somewhat strawman-like; the only genuinely competitive baseline is the authors' own MultiMesh-VP. Notably, no comparison to published diffusion-based sparse reconstruction methods (e.g., Oommen et al., Diff-SPORT) is performed on this data.

No inference-cost comparison. Diffusion sampling (T=20 reverse steps) on ~3×10^5-node graphs is substantially more expensive than a single forward pass of MGN/MS-MGN; since real-time monitoring is a stated motivation, the omission of wall-clock/compute comparisons against all baselines is a significant gap.

Observations are noise-free: sensor values are taken directly from the ground-truth RANS fields (Eq. 1 acknowledges noise η, but no noise or bias experiments are reported), which undercuts robustness claims relevant to real deployments.

The guidance weight γ=2.0 is fixed a posteriori from the sweep, and the sweep shows the optimum varies with observation density (γ=1.5 is best at 8000 obs); no adaptive or principled selection rule is offered.

Reproducibility is only partial: the code availability is a placeholder link, the dataset derives from an external CFD database (modelair.eu), and training used 4×A100 for 200k steps, which not all groups can replicate. Hyperparameters are documented, which helps, but the practical barrier is nontrivial.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (sparse-observation reconstruction of urban wind fields on unstructured meshes) using an industrial-scale, high-fidelity RANS dataset of a real Bristol neighborhood at Re ≈ 2×10^7, which is considerably more realistic than the toy/structured-mesh datasets common in this literature.

The formulation of classifier-free guidance as tempered posterior sampling (Sec. 2.2, Eq. 5) is a clear and useful framing that connects the diffusion approach to classical DA concepts (background/observation weighting), and it is supported by an empirical γ-sweep (Appendix C.1) showing the expected transition from prior-dominated to measurement-dominated sampling with an intermediate optimum.

The experimental design is reasonably thorough for its scope: three classes of baselines (supervised GNNs, reduced-order DA, and a diffusion baseline sharing the same multiscale backbone, which is important for isolating the contribution of the CFG formulation), held-out altitude slices, three sensor-sampling strategies, held-out sensor interpolation, CRPS-based ensemble evaluation, and a single-mesh ablation (Table 8) that quantifies the value of the multiscale hierarchy in the sparse regime.
Reproducibility support is good: architecture, message-passing equations, noise schedules, optimizer settings, and inference parameters are given in the appendices, and a code link is provided.

The paper is well written, and the limitations are discussed honestly (steady 2D slices from a single neighborhood, no PDE constraints, no temporal dynamics), rather than hidden; the impact statement appropriately frames the method as decision support.
weaknesses: The generalization claims are narrower than the abstract suggests. The 'held-out mesh geometries' are two altitude slices extracted from the same 3D domain of a single urban neighborhood; they share the same buildings, terrain, and city layout, differing mainly in obstacle cross-sections. There is no cross-city, cross-geometry, or off-mesh (interpolated) sensor evaluation, so the claim that the framework generalizes 'within the studied urban-flow setting' — while accurate — may be underappreciated by readers, and the broader scalability claim (other cities, 3D domains) is untested.

The theoretical interpretation of CFG as sampling from a tempered posterior is heuristic. The sensor-conditioned denoiser trained by dropout is not the exact score of p(u|y,G), so Eq. (5) is an approximation without error analysis or bounds; the paper presents it as an interpretation rather than a result, which is acceptable but limits the conceptual contribution beyond known results on guided diffusion for inverse problems.

Noise-free, on-mesh observations are assumed throughout (y is drawn directly from ground-truth fields); although Eq. (1) includes measurement noise η, no experiment tests robustness to sensor noise or bias, which is arguably the most critical robustness property for the real deployments the paper motivates.

Some baseline results are not fully explained: LCSVD and POD-3DVar report nearly identical values at 3000 and 8000 observations (e.g., RRMSE 0.354 vs 0.354, 0.368 vs 0.367), suggesting saturation by the reduced basis, but this behavior is not analyzed; and no inference-time or training-cost comparison is reported, which matters for claims of scalability against cheap classical methods.

The uncertainty evaluation is one-sided: CRPS is computed only for GenDA with no baseline comparison, and no calibration diagnostics (e.g., rank histograms or spread-error curves) are provided, so the claim that the ensembles are 'informative' is weakly substantiated.

Novelty is moderate: the components (MeshGraphNets-style multiscale message passing, EDM preconditioning, sensor-dropout CFG) are largely existing, and the closest related work (Giral et al., 2025; Diff-SPORT) is discussed but not compared against empirically; the contribution is primarily a well-executed integration and evaluation rather than a new method or new understanding.

The γ=2.0 setting is chosen from the same sweep used to report main results (Appendix C.1/Table 5), and the γ-sweep itself is evaluated on the test distribution, raising a mild concern about test-set-driven hyperparameter selection; no validation-split protocol is described.
SSIM computed on interpolated velocity-magnitude fields is a somewhat crude structural metric for unstructured flow data, and the calibration/interpolation choices for it are not discussed in depth.
